# Undo tablespace usage
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/FAQE/Undo+tablespace+usage
Updated: 2025-10-20T15:45:22.000+0900

- [Overview](#Undotablespaceusage-Overview) - [Version](#Undotablespaceusage-Version) - [Undo tablespace usage](#Undotablespaceusage-Undotablespaceusage) - [V$DISK_UNDO_USAGE performance view](#Undotablespaceusage-V$DISK_UNDO_USAGEperformanceview) - [Related bug](#Undotablespaceusage-Relatedbug)

# Overview

---

- Prior to ALTIBASE HDB 5.5.1, only ALLOC of undo tablespace could be checked, but USED could not be checked.
- This page describes how to use V$DISK_UNDO_USAGE to check actual undo tablespace usage.

#### ALLOC and USED of undo tablespace

---

- The undo tablespace is made up of segments, and segments are made up of smaller units called extents.
- When a change transaction occurs in a disk table, it is allocated in units of extents. Whenever an extent is newly allocated, the size of the undo tablespace ALLOC increases.
- When the transaction ends, the extent becomes reusable.
- However, if any of the extents within a segment are in use, even if there are reusable extents, all of the extents within that segment become unusable. (UNSTEALABLE EXTENT)
- Either the extent is used because a change transaction is executing, or the UNSTEALABLE extent is counted as USED for the undo tablespace.

# Version

---

This monitoring query is available in the version below.

- Altibase 5.5.1
- Altibase 6.1.1
- Altibase 6.3.1
- Altibase 6.5.1
- Altibase 7.1.1
- Altibase 7.3.1

# Undo tablespace usage

---

- ALLOC and USED may increase while a change transaction is being performed on the disk table.
- If the transaction is committed, the USED that is increased during the execution of the transaction is reduced.
- If the transaction is rolled back, the ALLOC and USED that have increased during the execution of the transaction will be reduced.

**Undo tablespace usage query**

```
SELECT T.NAME TBS_NAME
     , ROUND(D.MAX * PAGE_SIZE / 1024 /1024, 2) 'MAX(M)'                                                                        -- Max size of undo tablespace
     , ROUND((TOTAL_PAGE_COUNT * PAGE_SIZE) / 1024 / 1024, 2) 'TOTAL(M)'                                                        -- Total size allocated for undo tablespace
     , ROUND((U.TOTAL_EXT_CNT*PROP.EXTENT_SIZE)/1024/1024, 2) 'ALLOC(M)'                                                        -- Total of only 'used pages' excluding 'blank pages' among the allocated pages so far
     , ROUND(((U.TX_EXT_CNT+U.USED_EXT_CNT+U.UNSTEALABLE_EXT_CNT) * PROP.EXTENT_SIZE)/1024/1024, 2) 'USED(M)'                   -- Size of the EXTENT that cannot be reused or in use by the change transaction
     , ROUND((((U.TX_EXT_CNT+U.USED_EXT_CNT+U.UNSTEALABLE_EXT_CNT) * PROP.EXTENT_SIZE)/(D.MAX*PAGE_SIZE))*100, 2) 'USAGE(%)'    -- USED compared with MAX
     , DECODE(STATE,1,'OFFLINE',2,'ONLINE',5,'OFFLINE BACKUP',6,'ONLINE BACKUP',128,'DROPPED', 'DISCARDED') STATE               -- Tablespace state
     , D.AUTOEXTEND
  FROM V$TABLESPACES T
     , (SELECT SPACEID
             , SUM(DECODE(MAXSIZE, 0, CURRSIZE, MAXSIZE)) AS MAX
             , DECODE(MAX(AUTOEXTEND),1,'ON','OFF') 'AUTOEXTEND'
          FROM V$DATAFILES
         GROUP BY SPACEID) D
     , V$DISK_UNDO_USAGE U
     , (SELECT VALUE1 EXTENT_SIZE FROM V$PROPERTY WHERE NAME = 'SYS_UNDO_TBS_EXTENT_SIZE') PROP
 WHERE T.ID = D.SPACEID
   AND T.ID = 3 ;
```

**Example of output**

```
TBS_NAME                        MAX(M)      TOTAL(M)    ALLOC(M)    USED(M)     USAGE(%)    STATE           AUTOEXTEND
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SYS_TBS_DISK_UNDO               2047.99     302         122.25      84.25       4.11        ONLINE          ON
1 row selected.
```

| Column Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| TBS_NAME | Tablespace Name |
| MAX(M) | Maximum Size of Undo Tablespace |
| TOTAL(M) | Total Allocated Size for Undo Tablespace |
| ALLOC(M) | Total Used Pages (excluding free pages) among Allocated Pages |
| USED(M) | Size of Extents Used or Unusable Due to Active Transactions |
| USAGE(%) | Usage (USED vs. MAX) |
| STATE | Tablespace Status |
| AUTOEXTEND | Auto Extend Enabled up to Maximum Size |

# V$DISK_UNDO_USAGE performance view

---

| Column name | Data type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TX_EXT_CNT | BIGINT | Number of extents for a segment (Transaction Status Segment, TSS) that stores transaction status information. It is allocated when an update transaction occurs in the disk table. |
| USED_EXT_CNT | BIGINT | Number of extents in the undo segment being used in the transaction. When an update transaction occurs in the disk table, it is allocated as needed. |
| UNSTEALABLE_EXT_CNT | BIGINT | Number of extents that cannot be taken from other undo segments. The extent that belongs to the online undo segment and the extent that has header information. Contains the extent the transaction is accessing. Even if the undo segment has reusable extents, it cannot be taken from other undo segments. |
| REUSABLE_EXT_CNT | BIGINT | Number of reusable extents USED_EXT_CNT used during transaction progress increases as USED_EXT_CNT decreases when the transaction is committed. |
| TOTAL_EXT_CNT | BIGINT | The total number of extents allocated from the undo tablespace. When a transaction is rolled back, the extents used in the transaction are returned to the undo tablespace. When a transaction is committed, the extents used in the transaction are held in the corresponding undo segment. |

# Related bug

---

**Bug Description**

- Improved an issue where undo areas that cannot be reused were incorrectly counted as available space. (Extents corresponding to the UNSTEALABLE_EXT_CNT column were mistakenly calculated as usable extents.) (BUG-39985)

**Applied Versions**

- Altibase 6.1.1.4.9 or later

- Altibase 6.3.1.3.3 or later

- Altibase 6.5.1 or later

# Thread process debugging method
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/FAQE/Thread+process+debugging+method
Updated: 2021-04-05T13:30:06.000+0900

- [Overview](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Overview) - [Using pstack](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Usingpstack) - [How to use](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Howtouse) - [Example](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Example) - [Using dbx](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Usingdbx) - [How to use](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Howtouse.1) - [Example](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Example.1) - [Using gdb](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Usinggdb) - [How to use](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Howtouse.2) - [Example](#Threadprocessdebuggingmethod-Example.2)

# Overview

---

When a process on Unix consumes excessive CPU or hangs, the process debugging utilities provided by each Unix OS can help identify the cause by analyzing the currently running call stack.

Unix process debugging methods differ by utility and by Unix variant, so commands are often confused. This document explains simple commands for viewing each thread stack.

# Using pstack

---

`pstack` is provided by Sun, several other Unix variants, and Linux. It is useful for viewing the call stack of a running process by thread, and can be used when a database hang occurs.

## How to use

---

- Linux:

  ```
  shell> pstack processid
  ```

- Sun:

  ```
  shell> pstack -F processid
  ```

## Example

---

**Example**

```
[omegaman@as48-x64 ~]$ uname -a
Linux as48-x64 2.6.9-89.ELsmp #1 SMP Mon Apr 20 10:33:05 EDT 2009 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
[omegaman@as48-x64 ~]$
[omegaman@as48-x64 ~]$ whereis pstack
pstack: /usr/bin/pstack /usr/share/man/man1/pstack.1.gz
[omegaman@as48-x64 ~]$ ps -ef | grep altibase | grep omegaman
omegaman 16745 16454  0 13:55 pts/2    00:00:00 grep altibase
omegaman 22978     1  0 Dec04 ?        00:00:07 /home/omegaman/altibase_home/bin/altibase -p boot from admin
[omegaman@as48-x64 ~]$ pstack 22978      :22978 is  a process id of altibase
Thread 41 (Thread 1084229984 (LWP 22979)):
#0  0x00000039070c2f56 in __select_nocancel () from /lib64/tls/libc.so.6
#1  0x0000000000f40f4b in idvClockThread::run ()
#2  0x0000000000ef797c in idtBaseThread::staticRunner ()
#3  0x0000003907706137 in start_thread () from /lib64/tls/libpthread.so.0
#4  0x00000039070c9f03 in clone () from /lib64/tls/libc.so.6
Thread 40 (Thread 1094719840 (LWP 22980)):
```

# Using dbx

---

`dbx` is provided by AIX, HP, and Sun. You can check call stack information for a running process with the `dbx` command, and you can also check the stack for each thread in a core file.

This section describes the method used on AIX as an example.

## How to use

---

1. Check the process ID of the process in question: `shell> ps -eafl | grep altibase`
2. Attach to the process: `shell> dbx -a <pid of altibase process>`
3. View all thread information: `(dbx) thread`
4. View only individual thread information: `(dbx) thread current <thread number>` and `(dbx) where`
5. Detach: `(dbx) detach`

  Always execute the detach command to release the connected process. If you exit without detaching, the target process may also be terminated.
6. Exit: `(dbx) quit`

## Example

---

```
$ dbx -a 421920 Waiting to attach to process 421920 ... Successfully attached to altibase. warning: Directory containing altibase could not be determined. Apply 'use' command to initialize source path.

Type 'help' for help. reading symbolic information ...warning: no source compiled with -g

stopped in _event_sleep at 0x9000000004b6a84 ($t6) 0x9000000004b6a84 (_event_sleep+0xe8) e8410028 ld r2,0x28(r1) (dbx) where _event_sleep(??, ??, ??, ??, ??, ??) at 0x9000000004b6a84 _event_wait(??, ??) at 0x9000000004b6f5c _cond_wait_local(??, ??, ??) at 0x9000000004c305c _cond_wait(??, ??, ??) at 0x9000000004c3628 pthread_cond_timedwait(??, ??, ??) at 0x9000000004c3e38 run()() at 0x100187228 staticRunner(void*)() at 0x10007ea70 (dbx) list no source file (dbx) detach
```

# Using gdb

---

If `gdb` (GNU debugger) is installed, stack information for each thread can be checked by using `gdb`.

## How to use

---

1. Attach `gdb` to the target process: `shell> $gdb $ALTIBASE_HOME/bin/altibase process-id`
2. Print information for each thread: `(gdb) info threads`
3. Print the stack trace of all threads: `(gdb) thread apply all bt`
4. Switch to a specific thread: `(gdb) t 1` switches to thread 1.
5. Print the current thread's stack: `(gdb) bt`
6. Quit: `(gdb) quit`

## Example

---

```
$gdb $ALTIBASE_HOME/bin/altibase 34567 gdb> info threads 42 Thread 31 (LWP 4) 0x329614 in _poll () 41 Thread 30 0x300cf8 in _lwp_sema_wait () 40 Thread 29 0x300cf8 in _lwp_sema_wait () 39 Thread 28 (LWP 29) 0x329614 in _poll () 38 Thread 27 (LWP 28) 0x329614 in _poll () 37 Thread 26 (LWP 27) 0x329614 in _poll () 36 Thread 25 (LWP 26) 0x329614 in _poll () 5 LWP 28 0x329614 in _poll () 4 LWP 29 0x329614 in _poll () 3 LWP 30 0x300cf8 in _lwp_sema_wait () * 2 Thread 1 (LWP 1) 0x329614 in _poll () 1 LWP 1 0x329614 in _poll ()  gdb> thread apply all bt; Output stack trace of all threads Thread 2 (Thread 1 (LWP 1)): #0 0x329614 in _poll () #1 0x2f2548 in select_large_fdset () #2 0x286908 in __1cKidcManagerGselect6FpnGfd_set_pnOPDL_Time_Value__i_ () #3 0x978d8 in __1cMmmtThreadMgrIDispatch6M_nGIDE_RC__ () #4 0x945f4 in __1cGmmiMgrIMainLoop6F_nGIDE_RC__ () #5 0x929e0 in main ()  Thread 1 (LWP 1 ): #0 0x329614 in _poll () #1 0x2f2548 in select_large_fdset () #2 0x286908 in __1cKidcManagerGselect6FpnGfd_set_pnOPDL_Time_Value__i_ () #3 0x978d8 in __1cMmmtThreadMgrIDispatch6M_nGIDE_RC__ () ---Type to continue, or q to quit--- #4 0x945f4 in __1cGmmiMgrIMainLoop6F_nGIDE_RC__ () #5 0x929e0 in main () #0 0x329614 in _poll ()  gdb> t 1 ; Switch to thread 1 gdb> bt ; Output stack gdb> quit
```

# 1. Routine Checklist
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/1.+Routine+Checklist
Updated: 2025-09-24T09:12:59.000+0900

---

- [1.1 Routine Checklist](#id-1.RoutineChecklist-1.1RoutineChecklist)

Service delays can occur during operation because of sudden CPU overload. This chapter describes the items to check and the actions to take when delays caused by Altibase CPU overload occur repeatedly.

# **1.1 Routine Checklist**

The user needs the following history to determine whether the current CPU load is normal. Altibase does not provide its own CPU usage rate, so CPU usage must be checked with commands provided by the OS.

| Item | Collection Plan |
| --- | --- |
| Hourly/daily CPU utilization | Periodically record and manage the CPU utilization rate of the process by using the method provided by the OS. |
| Transaction throughput by time/day | Record and manage the transaction throughput of the application. If this is difficult, periodically collect and record the following information from `V$SYSSTAT` provided by Altibase.<br>```<br>select name,value from V$SYSSTAT where name in ( 'execute success count','prepare success count','prepare failure count');<br>``` |
| Whether the service thread is increased or decreased | Service threads may increase because sessions or workload are higher than usual. Check whether this pattern occurs.<br>`SELECT COUNT(*) AS THREAD FROM V$SERVICE_THREAD; SELECT COUNT(*) AS SESSION FROM V$SESSION;` |

It may be more convenient to record information collected at regular intervals in a file using the following shell script.

Since `EXECUTE COUNT` obtained from `V$SYSSTAT` is cumulative, calculate the increase per unit time as `(recent value - previous value)`.

```
# gettps.sh
ALTIPID=`ps -ef | grep $USER | grep  "bin/altibase -p boot"  | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}'`
MAXCOUNT=3
COUNT=0
INTERVAL=30
LOGFILE=altitps.log

do_getExecuteCount()
{
is -silent <<EOF
set linesize 1024;
set colsize 50;
set feedback off;
set heading off;
select 'RESULT='||( select count(*) from v\$session )
       ||'=' || ( select count(*) from v\$service_thread )
       ||'=' || ( select sum(value) from v\$sysstat where name in ( 'execute success count','prepare success count','prepare failure count') )
from dual;
EOF
}

while [ $COUNT -lt $MAXCOUNT ]
do
ALTICPU=`ps -o pcpu -p $ALTIPID | grep -v CPU`
EXECRESULT=`do_getExecuteCount`
SESSIONCNT=`echo $EXECRESULT | grep "RESULT=" | cut -d'=' -f 2| tr -d ' '`
THREADCNT=`echo $EXECRESULT | grep "RESULT=" | cut -d'=' -f 3 | tr -d ' '`
EXECCNT=`echo $EXECRESULT | grep "RESULT=" | cut -d'=' -f 4 | tr -d ' '`
echo  `date "+%Y%m%d %H%M%S: CPU USAGE="`$ALTICPU" SESSIONCNT=$SESSIONCNT THREADCNT=$THREADCNT EXECCNT=$EXECCNT"

sleep  $INTERVAL
COUNT=`expr $COUNT + 1`
done
```

When the above shell script is executed, the following output can be displayed.

```
$sh gettps.sh
20170203 150253: CPU USAGE= 12.3 SESSIONCNT=208 THREADCNT=16 EXECCNT=181813
20170203 150323: CPU USAGE= 24.8 SESSIONCNT=208 THREADCNT=10 EXECCNT=185834
20170203 150353: CPU USAGE= 32.1 SESSIONCNT=212 THREADCNT=15 EXECCNT=189865
......
```

With the above history information, the user will be able to create a history in the form of a table as follows. It is convenient to use the Excel cell calculation formula for the increment per unit time.

| Time(HH:MI:SS) | CPU (%) | Session / Thread | EXECUTE cumulative value | EXECUTE increase per unit time | TPS(Transaction per second) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 15:02:53 | 12.3 | 208/16 | 181813 | - | - |
| 15:03:23 | 24.8 | 208/16 | 185834 | 4021=(185834-181813) | 134=4021/30 seconds |
| 15:03:53 | 32.1 | 212/17 | 189865 | 4031=(189865-185834) | 134=4031/30 seconds |

With this type of data, it is necessary to first determine whether the difference in load between the normal point of time and the point of CPU overload is due to an increase in transaction throughput.

# 2. General Analysis Procedure
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/2.+General+Analysis+Procedure
Updated: 2025-09-24T09:13:16.000+0900

- [2.1 Has more transaction processing occurred than usual?](#id-2.GeneralAnalysisProcedure-2.1Hasmoretransactionprocessingoccurredthanusual?) - [2.2 Has a newly added service (application) occurred?](#id-2.GeneralAnalysisProcedure-2.2Hasanewlyaddedservice(application)occurred?) - [2.3 Problem analysis of the application in service](#id-2.GeneralAnalysisProcedure-2.3Problemanalysisoftheapplicationinservice) - [2.4 Problem caused by query execution cost increase due to query plan change](#id-2.GeneralAnalysisProcedure-2.4Problemcausedbyqueryexecutioncostincreaseduetoqueryplanchange)

In general, CPU utilization often increases for a small set of recurring causes. Therefore, checking whether the problem matches a known pattern step by step can be effective.

# 2.1 Has more transaction processing occurred than usual?

If the routine checklist items, such as `Session`, `Service Thread`, and `Prepare/Execute`, all increase while CPU usage increases, this can be considered a normal increase pattern.

Be careful to distinguish the following case from a normal pattern. Service threads may increase because of user-submitted queries or services that have not been verified, such as long-running queries or queries that cause a large volume of change operations.

This type of increase can occur because of the service thread's own load-balancing function.

The pattern itself can be normal, but the cause of the increased query activity still needs to be found. Queries executed manually by users are difficult to detect after the relevant time has passed, so periodically observe the server with the following query to find long-running queries.

```
-- Search for long-running queries whose execution time or result fetch time is 1 second or more
SELECT A.SESSION_ID,
       A.CLIENT_PID,
       B.QUERY,
       B.EXECUTE_TIME,
       B.FETCH_TIME
  FROM V$SESSION A,
       V$STATEMENT B
 WHERE A.ID = B.SESSION_ID
   AND (B.EXECUTE_TIME > 1000000 OR B.FETCH_TIME > 1000000);
```

# 2.2 Has a newly added service (application) occurred?

Because a newly added service is likely to be a direct cause, first analyze the execution plans of newly added queries. Then tune queries with high execution time and high access cost. Periodic observation is needed by using the long-running-query search method described above.

Both of the above cases usually mean that the service application's structure or the queries it executes were implemented inefficiently. For related background, see the CPU usage of Altibase query processing described below.

However, when users check the items in sections 2.1 and 2.2, the most common answer is "No". If there has been no change to the service configuration, the system, or the Altibase version, what is the cause of CPU overload?

To find the problem, analyze the currently running program and DB.

# 2.3 Problem analysis of the application in service

If CPU overload occurs even though there has been no change in the service operation configuration, the increase in data may have exposed a problem that already existed in an existing query.

For example, an index that worked smoothly when the data size was small may become inappropriate as the data size increases over time. In that situation, continued use of the existing index may cause CPU utilization to increase.

# 2.4 Problem caused by query execution cost increase due to query plan change

Altibase 4, Altibase 5, and some Altibase 6 versions (`6.1.1.6.1` or later) automatically execute optimizer statistics collection under certain conditions.

Statistical information is often updated because of data growth or DDL execution, such as an index change. In this case, the query optimizer may occasionally select an incorrect plan with a higher cost than the previous plan while selecting a new query plan.

Queries executed with such an inefficient plan can significantly increase access cost and cause CPU usage to increase. In many cases, the problem query is found with the long-running-query search query described above.

Therefore, when an abnormal CPU usage pattern occurs, it is effective to check the long-run query first with the monitoring query.

For an identified long-running query, check whether there is a problem with the plan by executing the command that shows the execution plan, or by querying the runtime plan stored in `V$PLANTEXT`.

To check query status, run the query status check query described in the "Altibase Monitoring Guide" document.

Altibase Monitoring Guide Document >> 3. Monitoring Elements and Monitoring Query >> 2.Statement (Shortcut: [2. Statement](https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/2.+Statement))

# 3. CPU Cost of Query Processing
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/3.+CPU+Cost+of+Query+Processing
Updated: 2025-09-24T09:13:34.000+0900

- [3.1 CPU load according to application program implementation type](#id-3.CPUCostofQueryProcessing-3.1CPUloadaccordingtoapplicationprogramimplementationtype) - [3.2 CPU Load by Data Scan](#id-3.CPUCostofQueryProcessing-3.2CPULoadbyDataScan) - [3.2.1 Data access of memory table](#id-3.CPUCostofQueryProcessing-3.2.1Dataaccessofmemorytable) - [3.2.2 Data access of disk table](#id-3.CPUCostofQueryProcessing-3.2.2Dataaccessofdisktable) - [3.3 Summary](#id-3.CPUCostofQueryProcessing-3.3Summary)

This chapter briefly describes where Altibase uses CPU during query processing.

# 3.1 CPU load according to application program implementation type

Altibase query processing is largely executed through the following processes.

1) Check sentence/grammar errors in the query

2) Check the existence of table/column used in the query

3) Establish an optimal execution plan

4) Access the data area and acquire or change data with the required operations

Among these processes, 1) through 3) are called Prepare-Validation-Optimization (PVO), and process 4) is called EXECUTE. In general, PVO accounts for about 60% to 70% of the entire query processing cost.

Based on the assumption above, repeatedly executing the same query in a `PREPARE-EXECUTE` pattern can be expected to cause inefficient CPU usage. Therefore, if the following values increase excessively in `V$SYSSTAT`, developers or operators should modify the application so that it does not repeatedly perform `PREPARE`, or should use the `PLAN-CACHE` function provided from Altibase 5.

```
iSQL> SELECT * FROM V$SYSSTAT WHERE NAME LIKE '%prepare%count%';
SEQNUM      NAME                            VALUE
---------------------------------------------------------------------
37          prepare success count           25522
38          prepare failure count           56
```

If the above values continue to increase significantly, part of the application is repeatedly performing `PREPARE`. The application can be found by combining `V$SESSTAT`, another performance view that shows `V$SYSSTAT` information in detail by session, with the `V$SESSION` table, which shows the process PID.

For more detailed information related to the above, refer to the "Altibase Development Guide".

# 3.2 CPU Load by Data Scan

## 3.2.1 **Data access of memory table**

Altibase's memory table is kept loaded in the physical system memory. The unit to be stored is stored in a page unit of 32Kbyte, and even within this page, it is divided into individual units (Slot) for each table suitable for record storage.

The problem is, when accessing a table in a full-scan format, the cost of accessing all the data in the table is very high. If such queries are executed in multiple sessions at the same time, the CPU usage rate will inevitably increase.

So, when using an index, does the CPU utilization necessarily decrease?

Not necessarily. The index of the memory table also exists in system memory. However, the memory table index does not contain the actual data value. Instead, it has the physical pointer value for the data location in system memory, and this pointer value is calculated with the index key value and stored in sorted converted-value form.

Therefore, the actual physical data indicated by the index is accessed every time to obtain and compare the data value. (This process may seem unreasonable, but it does not induce disk I/O in terms of performance, so it is possible to process more transactions by occupying the CPU even when other DBMSs require waiting time due to I/O.)

Therefore, even for queries using indexes, the CPU usage rate increases as the number of access-cost increases. Therefore, the user must make efforts to remove inefficient queries by monitoring the execution plan of queries executed in a service operation on a regular basis.

## 3.2.2 **Data access of disk table**

Understanding CPU usage for disk tables requires understanding CPU use on the I/O path. In general, an OS allocates a memory area called file cache and keeps frequently accessed file I/O data loaded in memory to preserve I/O performance. However, most RDBMS products achieve this effect by placing their own buffer in the middle, so if the file system supports Direct I/O, it is generally recommended to use Direct I/O instead of the file cache.

Buffered I/O uses CPU resources for read/write system-call processing in application code, and CPU resources are also consumed when the OS synchronizes file-cache contents to disk. At this point, the process waits until the I/O operation completes and CPU utilization may appear to decrease. However, service throughput can decrease because other applications cannot use those CPU resources during that time.

Conversely, when Direct I/O is used, the CPU delegates the I/O itself to the dedicated I/O channel. As a result, the CPU does not need to wait for I/O processing, other applications can use the resource, and the service can process relatively more work. However, compared with Buffered I/O, users may interpret the CPU usage rate as having increased.

For more detailed information on how to configure and operate Buffered I/O and Direct I/O, refer to the "Volume Configuration Guide Considering Disk I/O Bottleneck".

In summary, there is no single answer for whether Buffered I/O or Direct I/O is appropriate because both have trade-offs for CPU usage and performance. Configure them appropriately for the user's service environment.

# 3.3 Summary

All of the processes described above require CPU resources. Therefore, it is conceptually impossible for query processing itself to use little CPU while also producing high performance. However, users and developers can make Altibase use CPU efficiently while delivering the required performance.

# 4. CPU problems with other cases
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/4.+CPU+problems+with+other+cases
Updated: 2025-09-24T09:13:43.000+0900

- [4.1 Mismatch of DB and application program character set](#id-4.CPUproblemswithothercases-4.1MismatchofDBandapplicationprogramcharacterset) - [4.2 Increase of Service Thread](#id-4.CPUproblemswithothercases-4.2IncreaseofServiceThread) - [4.3 Effect of OS environment variable setting](#id-4.CPUproblemswithothercases-4.3EffectofOSenvironmentvariablesetting) - [4.4 Frequent DB connection attempts](#id-4.CPUproblemswithothercases-4.4FrequentDBconnectionattempts) - [4.4.1 Checking whether frequent DB access occurs](#id-4.CPUproblemswithothercases-4.4.1CheckingwhetherfrequentDBaccessoccurs) - [4.4.2 Selecting tuning target queries with profiling](#id-4.CPUproblemswithothercases-4.4.2Selectingtuningtargetquerieswithprofiling)

There are cases where performance is not at the desired level even though CPU is also not being used as much as expected. Consider the following cases for these phenomena.

# 4.1 Mismatch of DB and application program character set

When the character set (`NLS_USE`) setting differs between the DB and the application, Altibase performance can degrade and CPU usage can increase because of internal character-set conversion (encoding). In this case, resolve the problem by matching the character set between the DB server and the application.

```
# Query to check client's NLS_USE
iSQL> select id, comm_name, client_nls from v$session;

#  Query to check DB charset
iSQL> select * from v$nls_parameters;
SESSION_ID : 1
NLS_USE : US7ASCII <---- current client's character set
NLS_CHARACTERSET : MS949 <--- DB server's character set
NLS_NCHAR_CHARACTERSET : UTF8
NLS_COMP : BINARY
NLS_NCHAR_CONV_EXCP : FALSE
NLS_NCHAR_LITERAL_REPLACE : FALSE
1 row selected.
```

# 4.2 Increase of Service Thread

In the Altibase 4.3.x version range, cases have been reported where CPU usage increased because `Select-Poll` system calls increased as `Dedicated Thread` instances increased.

Altibase handles transactions through `Service Thread` instances that manage session connections. When a long-running query occurs or all `Service Thread` instances are in the `Executing` state, Altibase creates new `Dedicated Thread` instances in real time to process new connections or waiting transactions.

Newly created `Dedicated Thread` instances periodically check whether there is a transaction to process. In this process, Altibase issues more `Select-Poll` system calls and `sys(%)` increases within CPU usage.

The DB service thread state can be retrieved with the query below.

```
iSQL> select type,state, run_mode, count(*)
    2 from v$service_thread
    3 group by type,state, run_mode;
TYPE                  STATE       RUN_MODE   COUNT(*)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
IPC                   POLL        DEDICATED  1
SOCKET(MULTIPLEXING)  EXECUTE     SHARED     1
SOCKET(MULTIPLEXING)  POLL        SHARED     31
3 rows selected.
```

To handle this type of issue, one option is to increase the value of the `MULTIPLEXING_POLL_TIMEOUT` property. This reduces the number of system calls by increasing the execution interval of the `Select-Poll` system call.

Fundamentally, `Dedicated Thread` instances occur because of increased sessions, increased transaction load, many long-running queries, or lock contention. Users should consider improvements that eliminate these root causes.

# 4.3 Effect of OS environment variable setting

CPU usage can change depending on OS environment variable settings. Because Altibase adopts a multi-threaded structure, the related OS settings must be configured properly. These settings should not be understood as settings that reduce CPU usage, but as settings for cases where performance is not proportional to the CPU being used.

For more detailed information, please refer to the "Altibase Installation Guide" provided for each OS.

# 4.4 Frequent DB connection attempts

`V$STATEMENT` in Altibase contains execution information for queries executed by currently connected sessions. Therefore, in an application structure that repeatedly performs connect/disconnect, it is very difficult to find problematic queries from this information.

## 4.4.1 Checking whether frequent DB access occurs

This can be checked with the following query.

```
-- Identify whether frequent connect/disconnect is performed (frequent connect/disconnect causes performance reduction)
SELECT NAME, VALUE FROM V$SYSSTAT WHERE NAME LIKE ‘%logon cum%’;

-- Determine if CPU is used inefficiently by performing repetitive PREPARE process
SELECT NAME, VALUE FROM V$SYSSTAT WHERE NAME LIKE ‘%prepare%count%’;
```

## 4.4.2 Selecting tuning target queries with profiling

Moreover, application performance decreases by the cost of each connect/disconnect. Therefore, it is recommended to change the application structure so that work is processed while connected to the DB. If this is not possible, use the profiling function to find problematic queries, even at the risk of degrading DB performance.

```
ALTER SYSTEM SET TIMED_STATISTICS=1;
ALTER SYSTEM SET QUERY_PROF_FLAG=1;  -- Execute the function
ALTER SYSTEM SET QUERY_PROF_FLAG=0;  -- Terminate the function
```

All queries executed after the above function is enabled are recorded under `$ALTIBASE_HOME/trc/` with file names such as `xxxxx.prof` and the `*.prof` extension. This file is created as a binary file, so the user cannot check it directly. Convert it to plain text as follows.

```
shell>  altiProfile alti-13109987-0.prof > log1.txt
```

`altiProfile` is an analysis utility provided by Altibase. It can be used to create analysis files. Because the file records the executed query statements and detailed execution-time information, problematic queries that took a long time to execute can be found from that information.

For detailed usage of altiProfile, refer to AID's FAQ. (AID description page on how to log queries performed in Altibase: [http://aid.altibase.com/x/ygSL](http://aid.altibase.com/x/ygSL))

Use the profiling function carefully because it can degrade DB performance and can cause disk space shortage due to log recording.

# 5. Summary
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/5.+Summary
Updated: 2025-09-24T09:13:53.000+0900

- [5.1 Step-by-step inspection method](#id-5.Summary-5.1Step-by-stepinspectionmethod) - [5.1.1 Data collection for analysis](#id-5.Summary-5.1.1Datacollectionforanalysis) - [5.2 Cause analysis](#id-5.Summary-5.2Causeanalysis) - [5.2.1 Check whether it is related to the impact of application change](#id-5.Summary-5.2.1Checkwhetheritisrelatedtotheimpactofapplicationchange) - [5.2.2 Relevance to data increase and check whether there is any change in the query plan](#id-5.Summary-5.2.2Relevancetodataincreaseandcheckwhetherthereisanychangeinthequeryplan) - [5.2.3 Mismatch of DB and application character set](#id-5.Summary-5.2.3MismatchofDBandapplicationcharacterset) - [5.2.4 Increase of service thread](#id-5.Summary-5.2.4Increaseofservicethread) - [5.2.5 Effect of OS environment variables](#id-5.Summary-5.2.5EffectofOSenvironmentvariables) - [5.2.6 Frequent DB connection attempts](#id-5.Summary-5.2.6FrequentDBconnectionattempts) - [5.3 Navigation with OS utility](#id-5.Summary-5.3NavigationwithOSutility)

As described in previous chapters, for each item, this chapter summarizes how the user could routinely check and find the cause of the CPU overload.

# 5.1 Step-by-step inspection method

## 5.1.1 Data collection for analysis

Collect data to determine whether the current CPU load is normal. Use OS commands and the method described in "1.1 Routine Checklist" to collect information such as Altibase hourly/daily CPU usage and transaction throughput. Then determine whether the CPU usage increase is normal because transaction throughput increased.

## 5.2 Cause analysis

### 5.2.1 Check whether it is related to the impact of application change

If there is a newly added service (application) and the operation time of the newly added service and the time of an increase in CPU load amount coincide, it is necessary to check the relevance of the newly added service.

### 5.2.2 Relevance to data increase and check whether there is any change in the query plan

Check whether CPU usage increased because access cost increased as data accumulated over time. In older Altibase versions (`6.1.1` or earlier), statistics can be collected automatically under certain conditions. If the optimizer selects and uses a plan that is less efficient than the previous query plan because statistics were updated, the increased access cost can cause CPU usage to increase.

### 5.2.3 Mismatch of DB and application character set

When the character set (`NLS_USE`) differs between the DB and the application, Altibase performance can degrade and CPU usage can increase because of internal character-set conversion.

### 5.2.4 Increase of service thread

When dedicated service threads that handle session requests increase, `sys` CPU usage may increase because the `select-poll` system call periodically checks whether requests exist.

### 5.2.5 Effect of OS environment variables

There may be changes in CPU usage depending on the OS environment variable setting. Altibase adopts a multi-threaded structure, so it is necessary to properly set the related settings for the OS configuration.

### 5.2.6 Frequent DB connection attempts

Connecting to and disconnecting from the DB consumes DB resources, and in a structure that repeatedly connects and disconnects, problematic queries are difficult to detect. Because statements cannot be prepared and reused, this can also degrade query performance.

## **5.3 Navigation with OS utility**

Altibase adopts a multi-thread structure. Therefore, it is necessary to determine whether a specific internal thread is abnormally using a lot of CPU. In this case, the CPU usage and current state of each thread can be checked with the utility provided for each OS. For more detailed information, refer to the following document.

- "Utility Guide for each OS for Problem Analysis"
<!-- SOURCE_BLOCK_END source_id="AID-SRC-000255" block_id="BLOCK-000141" -->

## AID-SRC-000256 - Altibase CPU Overload Analysis Guide

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `source_id` | AID-SRC-000256 |

# Altibase CPU Overload Analysis Guide
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/Altibase+CPU+Overload+Analysis+Guide
Updated: 2021-02-22T13:18:22.000+0900

# **Overview**

---

The CPU load of the system is basically caused by the application program (User) and the kernel (Sys/Kernel). Cases created by the kernel are generally when events about system resource usage occur, and other cases are mostly used by application programs. In the case of Altibase, various algorithms are applied to process queries (transactions) created by users, and use of various system resources such as communication and replication with clients connected to DB, and disk I/O by processing data files occurs. CPU usage of both the User area and the Sys/Kernel area occurs.

This document describes what parts to examine when the CPU utilization rate occupied by Altibase increases, whether it is normal/abnormal, and how to solve it in abnormal cases.

It is recommended to refer to the following documents in advance.

- Altibase Development Guide
- Altibase SQL Tuning Guide
- Altibase Monitoring Query Guide

The test environment of this document is as follows.

- Altibase: Altibase version 6 or later
- OS: Linux (2.6.32-504.el6.x86_64)

For errors and improvements related to this document, contact the technical support portal or technical support center.

- Technical support portal: [http://support.altibase.com](http://support.altibase.com/) > Technical Knowledge > Q&A
- Technical support center: 02-2082-1114

# 3. Altibase Trace Logs
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/3.+Altibase+Trace+Logs
Updated: 2025-10-21T09:02:39.000+0900

- [Classification of trace logs](#id-3.AltibaseTraceLogs-Classificationoftracelogs) - [altibase_sm.log](#id-3.AltibaseTraceLogs-altibase_sm.log) - [altibase_qp.log](#id-3.AltibaseTraceLogs-altibase_qp.log) - [altibase_rp.log](#id-3.AltibaseTraceLogs-altibase_rp.log) - [altibase_dk.log](#id-3.AltibaseTraceLogs-altibase_dk.log) - [altibase_error.log](#id-3.AltibaseTraceLogs-altibase_error.log)

---

ALTIBASE records trace logs for important status information and errors by module under the `$ALTIBASE_HOME/trc` path.

## **Classification of trace logs**

The trace log recorded by ALTIBASE is as follows.

| Classification | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **altibase_boot.log** | Logs related to start/stop processes and overall DBMS operations |
| **altibase_cm.log** | Logs warning or trace messages from the communication module |
| **altibase_dk.log** | Logs related to DB link usage |
| **altibase_dump.log** | Debugging logs for errors occurring in the server |
| **altibase_error.log** | Logs related to errors occurring in the server |
| **altibase_ipc.log** | Logs information about resources created during IPC connection |
| **altibase_ipcda.log** | Logs information about resources created during IPCDA connection |
| **altibase_job.log** | Logs information related to the execution of JOB objects |
| **altibase_lb.log** | Logs warning or trace messages from the load balancer |
| **altibase_mm.log** | Logs generated during main module processing |
| **altibase_qp.log** | Logs related to DDL execution and query processing |
| **altibase_rp.log** | Logs related to replication operation status |
| **altibase_rp_conflict.log** | Logs related to replication conflicts |
| **altibase_sm.log** | Logs related to checkpoints and tablespaces |
| **altibase_snmp.log** | Logs warning or trace messages from SNMP |
| **altibase_xa.log** | Logs related to XA transactions |
| **killCheckServer.log** | Logs the results of executing the killCheckServer utility |

By default, the log files are circulated to altibase_xx.log-[1-10], including altibase_xx.log, to record 10 log files.

In the following, messages that are meaningful to the user are explained separately for each trace log.

### **altibase_boot.log**

---

The user must check altibase_boot.log first when an error occurs in DBMS. The orange color mark in the table is an error that the user must resolve.

| ERR-0108d (errno=0) License is invalid or expired. |
| --- |
| This error occurs when the license file is missing or incorrect when starting up. The user must check the license information in ALTIBASE and have it reissued if necessary. |
| ERR-01052(errno=13) Unable to invoke open() function on [/dbs/mydb-0-0] |
| This error occurs when the DB has not been created before the initial operation or when there is no permission to access the file. The user must create a DB or check if the user has permission to access directories and files. Alternatively, it may be the case that the data file was deleted by mistake by the user. In this case, a procedure to recover using a backup copy is required. |
| ERR-01052(errno=2) Unable to invoke open() function on [/dblog01/logfile536358] |
| During the Altibase operation phase, automatic recovery is performed, which occurs when the redo log file required for this process is damaged or does not exist. The user must request technical support from the ALTIBASE HQ. |
| ERR-0001c(errno=76) Unable to shutdown the communication channel |
| During the ALTIBASE shutdown phase, a warning message from the session-related cleanup process has no effect on the operation. |
| ERR-71019 (errno=104) Failed to invoke a system function, write() (read, accept, select) |
| This error occurs by an error in a disk or network. The user must check the file system or make sure there are no network problems. Alternatively, system calls may fail due to insufficient memory. |
| ERR-40029 (errno=16) Failed to invoke a system function, flock_trywrlock() |
| This error occurs when ALTIBASE is already running or ALTIBASE is restarting while it is already running. Or, it can occur when the system call fails due to insufficient memory. |
| ERR-11018 (errno=2) The version of data file for backup is not compatible with the version of storage manager. Backup DB => [ Version ID = 5.4.1, Bit = 64, Endian = LITTLE LogSize = 10485760 Transaction Table Size = 1024 ] Server=>[ Version ID = 5.4.1, Bit = 64, Endian = LITTLE LogSize = 10485760 Transaction Table Size = 2049 ] |
| This error occurs when attempting to recover with a data file that is incompatible with the ALTIBASE version currently in use while running with the backed-up data. Or, this occurs when attempting to run in a different state from the ALTIBASE setting value set at the time of backup. |
| [ERROR] first write () operation failed. errno=32 |
| This error occurs in the read/write system call while the session is disconnected, so the information is recorded in the form of a warning. This log is also recorded when an application forces a shutdown without a normal disconnection command. The operation is not affected. |
| ERR-7101d(errno=11) Protocol header error. (TCP 211.115.75.212:63847) Protocol processing failed. Close connection... |
| When a session accessed with the ALTIBASE connection port attempts to connect with a version that is not compatible with the ALTIBASE server version, the user must traceback with the output connection information to check whether the server/client versions are compatible. The operation is not affected. |
| ERR-4000f(errno=2) No Error Message Loaded |
| This error occurs when the files located in the `$ALTIBASE_HOME/msg/` path do not exist or are not compatible with the version. It can also occur when the user does not have read permission on that path. |
| [Notify : Query Timeout] Query Canceled by Server : Session ID = 102373 [Notify : Fetch Timeout] Session Closed by Server : Session ID = 80106 [Notify : Utrans Timeout] Session Closed by Server : Session ID = 80106 [Notify : Idle Timeout] Session Closed by Server : Session ID = 80106 |
| When TIMEOUT occurs due to QUERY/FETCH/UTRANS/IDLE TIMEOUT setting, a warning type log is recorded. If there is a problem, the session information is recorded along with the message, so the user must track the session and resolve it. |
| ERR-01027(errno=0) No more IPC channel (MAX=50, USED=50, BUFSIZE=65536) |
| This error occurs when attempting more IPC access than available resources. |
| [Warning] Memory allocation failed. Size:524320 Timeout: 0 ERR-61055(errno=12) Memory allocation failure |
| This error occurs when an internally required memory allocation fails due to insufficient memory. In this case, the user must determine the cause of insufficient memory and resolve it. If a case of insufficient swap memory occurs, ALTIBASE may terminate abnormally without warning. |
| ioctl() failed |
| This error occurs when there is a temporary problem with performing system calls between socket or disk I/O operations. Generally, this can be ignored, but it is recommended to check the network or disk. |
| WARNING : write error number : 0, file name : /dblog01/logfile537572, file handle : 440, intended size : 10485760, writed size : 10485760, or File Extending Failed. : The disk space has been exhausted. Error : Extending DataFile : from 0, size 10485760 |
| When creating a file that ALTIBASE requires due to insufficient disk capacity, this is a warning that the file could not be created normally due to insufficient capacity. The user must check the disk capacity and resolve it. |

### **altibase_sm.log**

---

`altibase_sm.log` is an important basis for determining whether checkpoints are being executed and whether long-running queries exist.

| [CHECKPOINT-BEGIN] |
| --- |
| This means the checkpoint has started. |
| Remove Online Log File at LFG [0]: File[220 ~ 227] |
| This message removes the transaction log files that are no longer needed for recovery as the checkpoint is performed. If it is continuously displayed as File [None], it is necessary to check whether there are any queries that have been executed for a long time or that there are no untransmitted parts due to the replication. |
| [CHECKPOINT-summary] BeginChkptLSN=[0,83,9820280], EndChkptLSN=[0,83,9820721], DiskRecLSN=[0,83,9820280] |
| When the checkpoint has been successfully completed, summary information about checkpoint performance information is recorded in the log. |
| [CHECKPOINT-END] |
| This means the checkpoint has been successfully completed. |
| Minimum LSN = [0,83,9824136] |
| The above value is the offset position of the log file being recorded of the transaction in progress. Therefore, if that value does not change and keeps the same value, it is necessary to check whether there is a query that is executed for a long time as in the Remove log above, or whether the replication is not transmitted. |
| Database-Level Backup Completed [SUCCESS] |
| This means the backup has been successfully completed. |
| DISK TABLESPACE .... DATABASE .... |
| This means the backup of disk tablespaces has been performed. |
| ~/loganchor0 BACKUP TO |
| This means that the backup of the log anchor has been performed. |
| MEMORY TABLESPACE DATAFILE …. BACKUP TO …. |
| This means that the backup of memory tablespace has been performed. |

### **altibase_qp.log**

---

In altibase_qp.log, a log of the DDL executed by the user and the case of changing DB property values with “ALTER SYSTEM” statement, etc. are recorded. They are classified as follows.

| [EXEC_DDL_BEGIN : create index T1_IDX on T1 (A)] |
| --- |
| Log indicating the start of DDL executed by the user |
| [EXEC_DDL_END : SUCCESS] |
| Log indicating the normal completing of DDL executed by the user |
| [EXEC_DDL_END : FAILURE] errorcode 1627549735. |
| Log indicating the error details of DDL executed by the user |
| [SET-PROP] CHECKPOINT_BULK_WRITE_PAGE_COUNT=[0] |
| Log indicating that the user changed a DB property setting value that affects the entire system |

### **altibase_rp.log**

---

`altibase_rp.log` records the operation state of replication.

| ERR-31017(errno=0) Replication not found |
| --- |
| This error occurs when the replication target objects do not exist when executing DDL. Therefore, it is necessary to check whether the replication target objects exist. |
| ERR-6200f(errno=16) [Sender] Stop sender thread REP1 at [9765213], Restart SN[9765207] |
| This log is created when the replication sender is explicitly stopped by the user |
| ERR-71017(errno=79) Failed to invoke a system function, connect() ERR-61012(errno=79) [Sender] Failed to connect to the peer server ERR-61022(errno=79) [Sender] Sender Sleep : 60 seconds [Sender] getNextLastUsedHostNo: from 192.168.1.81:53341 to 192.168.1.81:53341 ERR-61003(errno=9) Unable to read from a socket ERR-61012(errno=119) [Sender] Failed to connect to the peer server ERR-6100d(errno=119) [Sender] Failed to handshake with the peer server (Handshake Process Error) |
| This is the log when the replication sender cannot connect to the other side's server and attempts to reconnect.<br>It is necessary to check whether the other side's server, network status, and ALTIBASE are running properly. If the other party's replication is explicitly dropped, it is a normal error. |
| [Recovery Sender] Replication REP1 Start... at [60495917] |
| This is the log when the replication and the sender have started. |
| [Receiver] Replication REP1 Started ... |
| This is the log when receiver and replication have started properly. |
| RECEIVER:REPLICATION STOP MSG arrived! [ReceiverApply] REPLICATION STOP XLog arrived! Normal Stop! [Receiver] Replication REP1 Stopped ... |
| This is when the replication of other server is explicitly stopped by the user. |
| ERR-61047(errno=0) [Receiver] REP1 receiver has error in recvXlog() ERR-61048(errno=0) [Receiver] REP1 receiver has recvXLog error in run() ERR-6104b(errno=0) [Receiver] REP1 receiver is ended (by thr_exit) |
| This error occurs when the replication Receiver thread ends because of an error. |

### **altibase_rp_conflict.log**

---

Because `altibase_rp_conflict.log` records SQL statements when conflicts occur, it provides important clues for tracing replication problems.

|  |
| --- |
| ERR-61036(errno=0) [Receiver] err_not found in deleteXlog() ERR-61000(errno=0) The received record is not found in the database. |
| This conflict error is recorded when the corresponding record does not exist while executing a DELETE transaction received through replication. |
| ERR-61035(errno=0) [Receiver] An update conflict encountered. ERR-61001(errno=0) A conflict has been occurred while executing the received statement. |
| This conflict error is recorded when the before/after values of the corresponding record differ while executing an UPDATE transaction received through replication. |
| ERR-6103a(errno=0) [Receiver] err_not_found in updateXlog() ERR-61000(errno=0) The received record is not found in the database. |
| This conflict error is recorded when the corresponding record does not exist while executing an UPDATE transaction received through replication. |
| ERR-11058(errno=0) The row already exists in a unique index. |
| This error occurs when the corresponding record already exists on the receiving side while executing an INSERT transaction received through replication. Data with the same PK exists. |

The replication object name used in the examples above is `REP1`. Because the user-specified replication object name can differ, consider that when searching for errors and detecting replication Sender/Receiver operation state or conflict errors.

If a replication conflict occurs, data inconsistency may have occurred because the replication-environment considerations described above were not followed properly or because replication delay occurred. It is important to find the cause through the SQL statement left when the conflict occurred.

### **altibase_dk.log**

---

In altibase_dk.log, various information and errors that may occur in the environment using the Database Link are recorded.

| ERR-b1070(errno=0) ODBC problem occurred [0:IM002:[unixODBC][Driver Manager]Data source name not found, and no default driver specified] |
| --- |
| This error occurs when the specified data source name is not found or LD_LIBRARY_PATH is not set. |
| ERR-b1070(errno=239) ODBC problem occurred [327730:08001:Client unable to establish connection.] |
| This error occurs when it is not possible to connect to the Altibase server or when the odbc.ini environment variable is not set. This can be resolved by checking the server running state and adding odbc.ini to the environment variable. |

### **altibase_error.log**

---

`altibase_error.log` provides important clues for analyzing the cause when Altibase terminates abnormally.

| BEGIN-STACK-[CRASH]=====================================<br>Caller[0] 0000000000417208 Caller[1] 00007FFB5324FC20 Caller[2] 000000000042D81D Caller[3] 0000000000E72EEB Caller[4] 000000000042944A Caller[5] 000000000042AE2F Caller[6] 000000000042B7BC Caller[7] 0000000000EA65FB Caller[8] 00007FFB5324517A Caller[9] 00007FFB52214DC3<br>END-STACK===================================== [========= FATAL Terminated ==========] |
| --- |
| When Altibase terminates abnormally, the related trace log is recorded. In this case, compress the entire `$ALTIBASE_HOME/trc` directory and send it to Altibase headquarters or request technical support. |

# 1. Routine Check of Memory Usage
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/1.+Routine+Check+of+Memory+Usage
Updated: 2021-02-19T13:34:49.000+0900

- [How to check system memory/swap by OS](#id-1.RoutineCheckofMemoryUsage-Howtochecksystemmemory/swapbyOS) - [Routine Checklist](#id-1.RoutineCheckofMemoryUsage-RoutineChecklist) - [V$MEMSTAT](#id-1.RoutineCheckofMemoryUsage-V$MEMSTAT) - [Typical types of memory increase](#id-1.RoutineCheckofMemoryUsage-Typicaltypesofmemoryincrease)

---

Service delays can occur during operation because of sudden memory shortage. This chapter describes what to check and how to respond when memory shortage continues to occur.

# How to check system memory/swap by OS

---

Use OS commands to check available memory and determine whether the system has insufficient free memory.

The memory usage can be checked with the following OS command.

a. AIX

![svmon%E1%84%80%E1%85%A7%E1%86%AF%E1%84%80%E1%85%AA.png](https://docs.altibase.com/download/attachments/embedded-page/arch/1.%20Routine%20Check%20of%20Memory%20Usage/svmon%E1%84%80%E1%85%A7%E1%86%AF%E1%84%80%E1%85%AA.png?api=v2)

| Red Box | Description |
| --- | --- |
| size | The number of pages in the total physical memory. Actual 1 page is 4,096 bytes, so it is a system with 7936M of memory |
| inuse | The number of physical memory pages in use (Computational + Persistent) |
| free | The number of pages not in use in physical memory |
| pin | The number of pages of physical memory that cannot be swapped out |
| virtual | The number of pages created by VMM (Virtual Memory Manager) |
| pg space | The usage of paging space |

b. HPUX

Run `glance`, then press `m` to check memory.

![image2017-2-13%2014_21_10.png](https://docs.altibase.com/download/attachments/embedded-page/arch/1.%20Routine%20Check%20of%20Memory%20Usage/image2017-2-13%2014_21_10.png?api=v2)

Current physical memory 32.0GB - System 9.6GB + User 13.8GB + File cache 722MB - Buffer cache 0GB + Free 7.9GB (amount of available memory)

c. Linux

In Linux, memory usage status can be checked with the `top` command. The following is a sample `top` result. Among the displayed values, `free` and `cached` are the main items to check.

![image2017-2-13%2011_27_46.png](https://docs.altibase.com/download/attachments/embedded-page/arch/1.%20Routine%20Check%20of%20Memory%20Usage/image2017-2-13%2011_27_46.png?api=v2)

In Linux, available memory can be calculated as `free + buffers + cached`.

To analyze the memory capacity with the result of the top command above,

- Total physical memory: `16630888k`
- Actual memory in use (`used - cached - buffers`): `16559108k - 16034200k - 100516k = 424392k`
- Actual available memory (`free + buffers + cached`): `71780k + 100516k + 16034200k = 16206496k`
- Total memory (`actual memory in use + actual available memory`): `424392k + 16206496k = 16630888k`

The following is the result of the `free` command. The `-m` option specifies output in MB.

![image2017-2-13%2013_54_34.png](https://docs.altibase.com/download/attachments/embedded-page/arch/1.%20Routine%20Check%20of%20Memory%20Usage/image2017-2-13%2013_54_34.png?api=v2)

## Routine Checklist

The user needs the following history to determine whether current memory usage is normal. When a problem occurs, this history can be used as important information for tracking the cause by analyzing what increased compared with normal usage.

| Item | Collection Plan |
| --- | --- |
| Hourly/daily memory utilization | Periodically record and manage the memory utilization rate of the Altibase process by using the method provided by the OS. |
| Transaction throughput by time/day | Record and manage the transaction throughput of the application. If this is difficult, periodically collect and record the following information from `V$MEMSTAT` provided by Altibase.<br>```<br>select * from v$memstat order by alloc_size desc;<br>``` |
| Increase or decrease in the service thread | Service threads may increase because sessions or workload are higher than usual. Check whether this pattern occurs.<br>`SELECT COUNT(*) AS THREAD FROM V$SERVICE_THREAD; SELECT COUNT(*) AS SESSION FROM V$SESSION;` |

It may be more convenient to record information collected at regular intervals in a file using the following shell script.

Since `EXECUTE COUNT` obtained from `V$SYSSTAT` is cumulative, calculate the increase per unit time as `(recent value - previous value)`.

```
# gettps.sh
ALTIPID=`ps -ef | grep $USER | grep  "bin/altibase -p boot"  | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}'`
MAXCOUNT=3
COUNT=0
INTERVAL=30

do_getExecuteCount()
{
  is -silent <<EOF
  set linesize 1024;
  set colsize 50;
  set feedback off;
  set heading off;
  select 'RESULT='||( select count(*) from v\$session )
       ||'=' || ( select count(*) from v\$service_thread )
       ||'=' || ( select sum(value) from v\$sysstat where name in ( 'execute success count','prepare success count','prepare failure count') )
  from dual;
EOF
}
while [ $COUNT -lt $MAXCOUNT ]
do
  ALTICPU=`ps -o pcpu -p $ALTIPID | grep -v CPU`
  ALTIMEM=`ps -o pmem -p $ALTIPID | grep -v MEM`
  EXECRESULT=`do_getExecuteCount`
  SESSIONCNT=`echo $EXECRESULT | grep "RESULT=" | cut -d'=' -f 2| tr -d ' '`
  THREADCNT=`echo $EXECRESULT | grep "RESULT=" | cut -d'=' -f 3 | tr -d ' '`
  EXECCNT=`echo $EXECRESULT | grep "RESULT=" | cut -d'=' -f 4 | tr -d ' '`
  echo  `date "+%Y%m%d %H%M%S: CPU USAGE="`$ALTICPU" " MEM USAGE=$ALTIMEM" SESSIONCNT=$SESSIONCNT THREADCNT=$THREADCNT EXECCNT=$EXECCNT"
  sleep  $INTERVAL
  COUNT=`expr $COUNT + 1`
done
```

When the above shell script is executed, the following output can be displayed.

```
$ sh get.sh
20170213 110718: CPU USAGE= 7.1  MEM USAGE= 0.6 SESSIONCNT=1 THREADCNT=25 EXECCNT=1201
20170213 110748: CPU USAGE= 7.1  MEM USAGE= 0.6 SESSIONCNT=1 THREADCNT=25 EXECCNT=1202
20170213 110818: CPU USAGE= 7.1  MEM USAGE= 0.6 SESSIONCNT=1 THREADCNT=25 EXECCNT=1203
......
```

## **V$MEMSTAT**

V$MEMSTAT is a performance view of memory usage for each internal module provided by Altibase.

If the memory occupied by the Altibase process is large, the user can check Altibase's memory usage in detail with V$MEMSTAT.

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Query_Prepare | When executing SQL, memory is required during the prepare process to internally manage information such as SQL statement analysis, statistics information, execution plans, and bindings. In general, if an application executes SQL with a Prepare/Execute structure every time (Direct Execute method), memory usage for this item may increase.<br>If SQL is executed with the Prepare Execute method (1 Prepare + N Execute), memory usage for this item increases to some extent and then maintains a certain size during operation. This value is the total size of `Query_Prepare` used by all sessions. |
| Query_Execute | This is the memory size used to store data sort and intermediate result values during SQL execution.<br>This can increase when SQL is executed with a memory table or the `TEMP_TBS_MEMORY` hint. This value is the total size of `Query_Execute` used by all sessions. Memory is released when Altibase SQL execution ends. Therefore, in a normal case, it increases to some extent, then decreases, and maintains a certain size during operation. |
| Query_Binding | This is the memory size for storing binding variables during SQL execution. This value is affected by the binding variables used in one SQL statement. When the `PrepareStatement` is closed or the session is terminated, memory is returned, so it increases and decreases to some extent in normal cases and maintains a certain size during operation. Common examples of `Query_Binding` increase are as follows:<br>1) When statements increase rapidly<br>2) Binding for a very large data type<br>3) When `PrepareStatement` is not properly closed<br>4) When prepare statements are created repeatedly without limit while handling an exception |
| Storage_Memory_Manager | This is a space to store information for memory tablespace management and data in memory tables, and is the size of memory data residing in memory for Altibase's high-performance data processing. When memory data accumulates and grows, the value of this item increases. |
| Index_Memory | This shows the memory usage for indexes created on memory tables. An increase in this value means that memory index usage has increased. Memory can be cleaned up by removing indexes that consume a large amount of memory. |
| Storage_Disk_Buffer | This is memory used by the disk buffer manager. It is the space used to process data by buffering disk tablespace data in memory. If this space is insufficient, disk page in/out occurs frequently, which can degrade performance. |

## **Typical types of memory increase**

The memory increase of Altibase can be organized as follows based on the "Routine Checklist" described above.

1. When data in the memory table is increased
2. When the number of executing SQL statements increases
3. When it is increased by the MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) technique
4. When the deletion of aging target information is delayed

Let's take a closer look at the causes and measures for these cases in the next chapter.
<!-- SOURCE_BLOCK_END source_id="AID-SRC-000276" block_id="BLOCK-000144" -->

# 2. Causes and resolution for increase of Altibase process memory usage
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/2.+Causes+and+resolution+for+increase+of+Altibase+process+memory+usage
Updated: 2021-02-19T13:38:33.000+0900

- [1. When data in the memory table is increased](#id-2.CausesandresolutionforincreaseofAltibaseprocessmemoryusage-1.Whendatainthememorytableisincreased) - [2. When the number of executing SQL statements increases](#id-2.CausesandresolutionforincreaseofAltibaseprocessmemoryusage-2.WhenthenumberofexecutingSQLstatementsincreases) - [3. When it is increased by the MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) Technique](#id-2.CausesandresolutionforincreaseofAltibaseprocessmemoryusage-3.WhenitisincreasedbytheMVCC(Multi-VersionConcurrencyControl)Technique) - [4. When the deletion of aging target information is delayed.](#id-2.CausesandresolutionforincreaseofAltibaseprocessmemoryusage-4.Whenthedeletionofagingtargetinformationisdelayed.)

---

Memory increases caused by processes other than Altibase are not covered in this document. This chapter describes how to respond to increases in Altibase process memory usage.

As mentioned in the previous chapter, the memory increase of Altibase can be organized as follows:

1. When data in the memory table is increased
2. When the number of executing SQL statements increases
3. When it is increased by the MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) technique
4. When the deletion of aging target information is delayed

## **1. When data in the memory table is increased**

The trend of memory data usage increase can be checked with the SQL statement below.

```
set linesize 100;
set colsize 30;
SELECT A.TABLE_NAME
     , (B.FIXED_ALLOC_MEM + B.VAR_ALLOC_MEM) ALLOC
     , (B.FIXED_USED_MEM + B.VAR_USED_MEM) USED
  FROM SYSTEM_.SYS_TABLES_ A ,
       V$MEMTBL_INFO B
 WHERE A.TABLE_OID = B.TABLE_OID
   AND A.TABLE_TYPE = 'T'
 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

Among the results from the above query, 'Alloc' includes both space where data is stored and the available space. ('Used' means only space where data is stored.)

If the user deletes around `900M` after loading `1G` of data, the table still has `1G` of allocated space, `100M` of used space, and the remaining `900M` as empty space usable only by that table.

The part that confuses many Altibase users is this `900M`. Because the data was deleted, users often expect this space to be freed by Altibase or the OS and expect memory usage to decrease.

Most OS memory management structures do not immediately return memory to the OS even if a program frees memory that was allocated once. In practice, they generally reserve the freed area in memory and use that free area when another application runs out of memory. In other words, because memory allocation and deallocation are costly, frequent memory allocation/free operations are avoided as much as possible.

This algorithmic concept applies equally to Altibase. Altibase also keeps the used space as reusable space in the table even if data is deleted.

If the user finds such a table, take the following actions.

1. Compact the table. Memory tables are allocated space from a memory tablespace. However, if space increases because a large amount of data was loaded into and deleted from one table, other tables in the same memory tablespace may not have enough allocatable space. Unused space in a table can be returned so that other tables in the same memory tablespace can use it. This is called compaction.

  ```
  ALTER TABLE table_name COMPACT;
  ```
2. Restart Altibase.

  These actions make it possible for other tables in the same memory tablespace to be allocated space. However, the memory usage occupied by the OS still does not decrease. In this case, restarting Altibase can have the same effect as reducing memory usage for the following reason.

  In the restart process, the data pages of all memory tablespaces are loaded into memory, but empty pages that are not actually written to are not loaded into memory, thus reducing memory usage.

  If it is difficult for the user to perform compaction on each table, the compaction effect can be obtained by restarting Altibase during regular preventive maintenance (PM).

## **2. When the number of executing SQL statements increases**

The user can periodically check the number of queries recorded in `V$STATEMENT`. The queries recorded in `V$STATEMENT` are not exact because only queries executed by currently connected sessions are recorded, but they are useful for estimating the approximate count.

In this case, there is no special action for the user to take if the increase is caused by queries required for business purposes. However, the following items often need to be checked with the developer.

1. Check whether all queries are closed after use. In general, after a query is used, the object for that query must be closed.

  Ex) JAVA/JDBC

  ```
  Connection cn;
  prepareStatement ps;
  ps = cn.prepareStatement ("select…");
  …
  ps.close();
  ```

  If a statement such as `ps.close` does not exist in the above code, Altibase internal modules such as `Query_Prepare` continue to maintain memory for the query. If this situation repeats, memory continues to be used unless the session ends. Even if Altibase frees memory that was used once, the OS does not immediately reclaim it, and as a result memory usage remains increased. Therefore, check whether objects used for query execution are released normally.
2. Check whether similar queries continue to be used. Consider the following example.

  ```
  SELECT 1 FROM DUAL WHERE C1 = 1;
  SELECT 1 FROM DUAL WHERE C1 = 2;
  SELECT 1 FROM DUAL WHERE C1 = 3;
  ```

  The above queries can be handled with one statement by replacing them with a statement such as `SELECT 1 FROM DUAL WHERE C1 = ?` and developing the application so that only the variable value in the query condition changes.

  If similar queries as above are accumulated and executed, the current version of Altibase allocates memory by analyzing each query as a different query.

## **3. When it is increased by the MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) Technique**

The MVCC technique refers to a general DBMS concurrency control method that improves performance by preventing read and change operations from waiting for each other. Currently, Altibase memory tables operate by creating a copy of a record at the time of a change operation and recording the changed information in that copy.

Therefore, when a record is changed, the original and the copy exist together. At the time of deletion, there is no memory increase of this type; an increase may occur due to aging delay.

This means that when a large change operation is performed, copies are created for as many records as are targeted by the change operation. This is a trade-off in which resource usage increases in exchange for high performance.

This copy is created in the space of the table. Therefore, when a large amount of change operation occurs, the usage of the table increases. If there is empty space in the table, the corresponding space is used, and if there is not enough space, space is allocated from the tablespace and used.

The user should use the usage result for each table to identify tables where the difference between `Alloc` and `Used` is excessive, and take action if abnormal usage is found during operation. The available measures are table compaction or restart, as described earlier. Also, because large change operations are generally not recommended for DBMS work, perform change operations in batches of a certain number of records.

For example, if ten million records must be changed, divide the work into units of tens of thousands of records and perform the changes in batches by using the `LIMIT` clause.

## **4. When the deletion of aging target information is delayed.**

The original record becomes a deletion target because the copy created by MVCC becomes the final record at commit time.

If a rollback occurs, the copy becomes the deletion target. These records to be deleted are called `Old Version` or `Garbage Data`. The deletion operation is internally called aging, and an internal module called GC (Garbage Collector) handles it.

The problem is that there may be cases in which the deletion targets cannot be deleted for some reason. If this state persists, the deletion targets will continue to accumulate, which may cause an increase in memory usage.

Whether GC is aging records normally can be checked with the following query.

```
SELECT ADD_OID_CNT, GC_OID_CNT FROM V$MEMGC;
```

`ADD_OID_CNT` refers to the targets that transactions handed over for aging.

That is, it is the same as the number of transactions that requested aging. `GC_OID_CNT` means the number of aging targets processed by GC.

If the above values continue to change, GC can be considered to be working normally even if processing is delayed. However, if `GC_OID_CNT` does not increase at a specific point in time, a problem can be considered to have occurred.

The GC module can delete the record only if the record to be deleted is not referenced by any transaction, and the delete target list can be deleted only in the order requested.

Therefore, if a GC problem is suspected, the issue is usually that a transaction still remains unfinished. Find and clean up the corresponding transaction.

The transaction can be found with the following query.

```
SELECT A.SESSION_ID,
       B.QUERY
  FROM V$TRANSACTION A,
       V$STATEMENT B,
       V$MEMGC C
 WHERE A.ID = B.TX_ID
   AND (A.MEMORY_VIEW_SCN = C.MINMEMSCNINTXS
        OR A.MIN_MEMORY_LOB_VIEW_SCN = C.MINMEMSCNINTXS);
```

When the above query is executed, it displays information about the problematic query, including the monitoring query itself.

If a query other than the monitoring query is displayed and its execution time is excessive, tune that query. If the user did not terminate normally after executing the query, check the program source and make it terminate normally.

※ Memory increase related to MVCC and GC is limited to the memory table.

# Altibase Memory Usage Increase Analysis Guide
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/Altibase+Memory+Usage+Increase+Analysis+Guide
Updated: 2020-08-18T16:12:03.000+0900

# Overview

---

Problems caused by increased system memory usage are usually caused by application programs (users) or by data growth in memory tablespaces.

Queries used by applications can load database memory and lead to insufficient available memory. When data is managed in memory tablespaces for high-performance Altibase processing, accumulated data can also increase storage space usage and lead to insufficient available memory.

This document examines the memory areas occupied by Altibase and describes how to respond when Altibase uses memory abnormally.

It is recommended to refer to the following documents in advance.

1. [Altibase Developer Guide](http://aid.altibase.com/x/2gRw)
2. [Altibase SQL Tuning Guide](http://aid.altibase.com/x/owGr)
3. [Altibase Monitoring Query Guide](http://aid.altibase.com/x/j4KZ)
4. Altibase Memory Tablespace Management
5. Altibase MVCC & GC

The test environment of this document is as follows.

- Altibase: Altibase version 7 or later
- OS: Linux (2.6.32-504.el6.x86_64)

For errors and improvements related to this document, contact the technical support portal or technical support center.

- Technical support portal: [http://support.altibase.com](http://support.altibase.com/) > Technical Knowledge > Q&A
- Technical support center: 02-2082-1114

# 1. Altibase Server Monitoring Overview
Source: https://docs.altibase.com/display/arch/1.+Altibase+Server+Monitoring+Overview
Updated: 2025-09-24T08:56:05.000+0900

- [Monitoring Classification](#id-1.AltibaseServerMonitoringOverview-MonitoringClassification) - [Data Dictionary](#id-1.AltibaseServerMonitoringOverview-DataDictionary) - [Monitoring Method](#id-1.AltibaseServerMonitoringOverview-MonitoringMethod)

This chapter describes the basic concepts required to monitor an Altibase server.

## Monitoring Classification

---

Altibase is a DBMS. DBMS monitoring can be classified into three categories as follows.

**This document guides users through the monitoring queries needed for 'internal monitoring'.**

- Internal Monitoring: Monitoring inside the DBMS by querying the data dictionary.
- External Monitoring: Monitoring outside the DBMS by using OS commands.
- Trace Log Monitoring: Monitoring the trace logs recorded by the DBMS.

## Data Dictionary

---

The Altibase data dictionary consists of two types that summarize and store all information about the database so that DBMS can be used efficiently.

- **Meta Table**

  These tables are created automatically at database creation time to manage database objects. They are owned by the system administrator user `SYSTEM_`, and general users can only query them with `SELECT`.
- **Performance View**

  A performance view returns Altibase internal status information at `SELECT` time, so it can be used to obtain the latest server status. Performance views are also read-only, and their prefix is `V$`.

## Monitoring Method

---

Monitoring methods commonly used in the field are as follows.

- Writing shell scripts
- Writing applications
- Using utilities
